headline: Holgate's inside cut is stacking bunker — blues and the first real bass are behind them
subhead: The new moon squeeze did what we said it would: bait tightened against the beach and the fall bite is finally waking up from Barnegat Light to Little Egg.
body_markdown:
Walk the beach at low light this week and the story is written in the sand before you even string up a rod. The cut that opened south of Holgate's dune line during the last blow has deepened and swung a few degrees south, and there's a hard rip line running off the point of it on the outgoing that's holding color different from the water on either side — a green-brown edge where the bunker have been balling up tight enough to dimple the surface. That's the tell. Bait isn't drifting loose anymore. It's stacking, and stacked bait against structure in mid-September means one thing on this stretch of coast.

We flagged this exact setup last week — said the new moon's tidal squeeze would push bunker pods hard against the beach and inlet and trigger the first real blitzes of the fall, and that's exactly what's unfolding right now from Barnegat Light down through Beach Haven. The moon's still throwing extra push through the system a few days past new, and that bigger tidal range is doing the work — bait gets pinned against bars and jetty rock on the last two hours of the ebb, and the blues that have been scattered and picky all summer are suddenly not picky at all.

Bluefish are the story of the week, no argument. Cocktail blues to 4 pounds and better mixed in are running the surf line from the Ship Bottom jetties down to the Holgate cuts, showing up hard on the last of the outgoing when bunker peanuts get funneled off the bar edges. Poppers and darters are getting looks, but the fish that are committing are eating metal — 2 to 3-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks worked with a fast, erratic retrieve through the froth where the birds are working. If you see gulls diving tight to the beach rather than working a wide area, that's peanut bunker getting pinned, and that's where to put your first cast, not out past it.

Stripers are trailing this pattern, not leading it yet, which tracks with where we are in the calendar. The fall migration is visibly moving from Raritan Bay on down the coast, and LBI is starting to see early committed fish rather than just stragglers picking at the edges. Best action so far has come on the same tide stage as the blues — last two hours of the ebb into the start of the new flood — with fish showing at Holgate's southern cuts and along the outer bar off Beach Haven. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along the bottom drop-off, are outproducing plugs right now because the bass are still keying on smaller peanut bunker and mullet rather than committing fully to a full-size baitfish profile. Keep the retrieve slow and let it stall on the drop.

Inside the system, Little Egg Inlet and the flats off Graveling Point are worth the run if the ocean surf is blown out — and this week it has been rough more often than clean, with 3 to 4-foot swell and short period chop keeping the beach sloppy on a south wind. That pushes activity into the inlet and bay side, where fluke are still working but scattered rather than concentrated, exactly the pattern we called a week ago. The bite hasn't collapsed, it's just thinned out as bait spreads along the beach instead of holding tight to structure. Drifting the deeper holes off Graveling Point and the edges of the Mullica channel on the last of the incoming is still producing keeper fluke in the 18 to 22-inch range on Gulp Swimming Mullets in white or pink shad, bounced slow off bottom in 12 to 18 feet. Live killies fished on a light fluke rig off the bay side docks near Beach Haven are also worth a few extra fish if you can get them.

Weakfish and kingfish have been quieter than the blues and bass, which is normal for this point in September — both tend to show better in the cooler shoulder weeks either side of the peak fall run, and there's no strong signal on either right now worth chasing hard.

Looking at the next few days, the tidal range is still elevated coming off the new moon, which should keep the bunker pods tight against the beach and the blitz windows active on the outgoing tide, particularly around Holgate and the Ship Bottom jetties where the cuts are holding bait. If the wind swings more out of the northeast and knocks the swell down even a foot, the ocean beach bite should sharpen up fast because that bunker will hold instead of getting pushed around by chop. If you've only got one tide to fish this weekend, make it the last two hours of the ebb at Holgate's inside cut — that's where the bait, the current, and the structure are lining up right now. Keep an eye on the bird activity before you commit to a spot; this bite is moving day to day with the bait, not settling into one fixed piece of structure yet. That should change over the next week or two as more bass push down the coast and start locking onto these bunker schools for good.
